utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think there are a few things left from last week we have to do. utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I take it that includes the 92 bis argument. That will come at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we only received now the statements and it's a bit difficult for us -- of course we could hear oral argument, but since these documents arrived today -- no, last Friday, but it was three binders and I was not able to read them all over the weekend. And I think we have a better idea of what the 92 bis is about if we have seen the statements. So I'd rather -- yes, unless this disturbs you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at all. Okay. So Madam Registrar, could you please help us, guide us, through the documents used during the examination of Mr. Kucanin.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2792 is the photo file bearing on the first page the ERN number 0028-4265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any objection, if not, it is admitted into evidence. Next one, please.

utterances.text: P1840 under seal, the record of on-site investigation by Sarajevo CSB. And P1840.1 is the English translation, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Exhibit P2790, an official note, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Interior, date 22/07/1994. And the English translation, P2790.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Yes, that's admitted in evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections -- Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the date of that document, which is the 27th of July, 1994, it therefore being many months after the relevant date for the incidents which took place in Alipasino Polje. It was to those incidents which the Defence intimated this document relates. So I object on that basis, but it's not a strong objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin or Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. I checked the documents which were produced. It is quite possible that there is a problem concerning the date because there are two sets of documents, the first refers to the 20th of July, 1993, and therefore I believe there would be no objections to it. The other one is of the 27th of July, 1993, likewise. If that is not the case, then obviously it is a question. But with regard to the document that we are talking about, it is D54. Yes, I do not think that it is possible for a Defence because these documents have not been translated into English by the Prosecution. We could not find the documents which apply to the 9th of July, 1993, which is I believe the date of the incident. And a short time after the incident and during the period of the indictment, there are certain events which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further observations. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the relevant date in fact is the 9th of November, 1993. So it's some eight months prior. The reason I said that I don't make it a strong objection is the document as tendered is clearly of little weight. I understood my friend to be suggesting that in fact the date of this document which he seeks to tender is not the date which appears on it in the top left-hand corner. One doesn't need to understand B/C/S to see that the date of the document is 27.07.1994. If my friend is suggesting that the date of the document is in fact 1993, I think that should be made clear at this stage before it's tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I think this is not a linguistic matter to all, of course. One does not need the knowledge of B/C/S. It is simply that within the means of the Defence to show what happened at a particular period of time. And around that period of time if there were some elements, it is quite possible that they also sometime before that. And Mr. President, this is a time of war, and we -- one does not move brigades or armies just like that. I mean, a brigade will have 2.000 people. And therefore, I hope that the Prosecution has heard all of the -- all of this in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do I understand you well, that you accept to be the date of this document, the 27th of July, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The date was not manipulated by the Defence. It is the date on the document. Therefore presumably, it is the date which is on the document, and as the Prosecution says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, partly because of the strength of the objection of the Prosecution, we'll admit it into evidence. But as I have indicated before, that the probative value of this document for something that happened many, many months before is, of course, of a relative character. Madam Registrar, this document, D54, is admitted into evidence. Then the next document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D55, document bearing ERN number 0205-6280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's a similar objection. The date of this document is some three months after the relevant event. I would add to that the fact that the relevant portion relied upon by the Defence translates as a reference to a "command point of 102 Motorised Brigade in Alipasino Polje area." In other words, there's no suggestion in the document as to where precisely within that large part of Sarajevo the command point was. The Defence seem to be suggesting that because there was a command pointed in Alipasino Polje area, that therefore the mortar shell impacting either on the school or at the point 2 or 300 metres away is explicable as having a military objective. Essentially I say that again it's of such little weight as to be of no assistance to the Trial Chamber, but again if it is admitted then the same argument applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I see that this morning the position of the Prosecution is bis repetita placent, it seems that they do it more often than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not quite clear to me the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. President. I said that the position of the Prosecution this morning is bis repetita placent, and I repeat, those who do more, do less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With a similar observation as I made in respect of D54, the document is admitted into evidence. Then, Madam Registrar, we come to D56. Yes, could we do 56, 57, and 58 in one. Could you please, Madam Registrar, yes, because they seem to be similar documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: None of these documents bear any ERN numbers. D56 bears the date 19.7.1993, and 20.7.1993. D57, a report, UNPROFOR report. And D58 is a portion of an UNPROFOR report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps for the clarity of the transcript, they are all parts of what seems to be annex Roman VI, page 583, page 591, and page 592. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I trouble the Registrar for either a copy or at least a quick look at D56. I don't seem to have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there have been some difficulties as far as numbering is concerned. It is page 583 and 584. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you now clarify the source of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, because of the size, I did not bring all the whole set of the documents that we discussed on Friday. But I believe these are the military reports of the UNPROFOR. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what I will do, Mr. President, is as follows: To indicate the source, because last week I was called -- had somebody told me last week, we should be asking for the source then I would have brought everything. But it is now that I'm asked this and I will therefore do as follows: I will copy the page, the cover page of the document that we have, and that is the annex, I believe. I believe, I repeat, regarding the final report of the UNPROFOR. I will photocopy this particular page. I will communicate it both to the Prosecution and to the Registry so that all the questions which are relative to the source of the document and how it was produced are fully clarified. This seems to me the logical procedure, to provide the cover page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I wondered whether these annexes to the report of Committee of Experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: They appear to be that, Mr. President. And in fact I did ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin in open court last week, last Friday, to indicate the source but I'm not too fussed by that at the moment. These documents relate to the little girl being shot dead on the 20th of July, 1993. I object to their tender and I do so strenuously on this occasion for the reason that there is simply no connection at all. My learned colleague suggested on Friday that the connection was that there was fighting, and that was the English translation, in Sarajevo, therefore implying that the bullet could have been a stray one in the context of shooting by both sides. When one examines these documents more closely, one sees that there's no reference to outgoing fire at all, more importantly, the fighting was in the vicinity of Mount Igman which is to the southwest of the city whereas this incident occurred in the north or northeast. There is simply no connection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with pleasure, Mr. President. It takes me a few seconds. It did not escape -- your Chamber surely noticed that an appeal is made, an urgent appeal is made to the International Community by the Bosnian Presidency to say that there would be a general attack on the city. Now, this attack began on -- from Mount Igman. That is quite true. But in the military technique, when there is an attack as such, and I believe that is something that our Prosecution failed to notice, one has to move the soldiers in order to bring them to the front, and there are forces which go through the city. And when troops passed, what happens? Simply when the soldiers pass by one place or another place, obviously then they can be the contact. And it happened -- it also happened by night because there was fighting at night, major fighting at night unfortunately when this child was killed. We know Mr. President that what is happening, that there must be movement of troops. And this is proven by these troops. And therefore we think that this is the probative value of this document, and therefore so with which the Prosecution objects to the adoption of this document seems to me precisely one of the elements which is indicative of the probative value of this document. And here the date is fully exact, not only with regard to that date but also with regard to the night. And therefore the day which follows the day after the fact, it shows that all that week nothing could be done by the police, by the police, because presumably this whole area was the theatre of fighting. As I said, this is this gap between the 20th of July and 29th of July, 1993. And it seems to me that this document shows that the reason why the police could not reach the area was because of this fact, and that is why the Bosnian government launched that appeal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a decision on the admission into evidence of these three documents after the break. Mr. Ierace -- yes, we have still another document, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D59, under seal. Photocopy of three photographs and a cover page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please put your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 00269223. D59 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could I just see the exhibit. Yes, thank you. Since there's no objection, they are admitted into evidence. Then I think we dealt with all the documents used during the examination of Mr. Kucanin, and we will then proceed with your next witness. And protective measures involved are voice -- face distortion as far as I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you entertain at the outset --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm sorry, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honour. I would first like to make an oral application for protective measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can it be done in open session or do we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It can be done in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These witnesses only require facial distortion so it is not broadcast on television. The first witness is witness Mirza Sabljica. He is on the schedule for this week. He has arrived, and he indicates that as a result of his present occupation now, he has to travel quite extensively through the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he fears that if his is broadcast, then persons might recognise him. And it might adversely affect the operations of his business. That, briefly, is his concern. The next witness is the witness Esrema Boskailo. She lives in Sarajevo, but her father lived in Republika Srpska. He has recently died, and the family house now belongs to her, and she has to travel to Republika Srpska to look after affairs in respect of that house. Her concern is that if her face is broadcast and she is recognised, then she or her family, she has three children, may be in physical danger as a result of her being recognised as a witness here. And those are her concerns. And she also only asks for a facial distortion, so that her face is not broadcast. No distortion in Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the main reason is to avoid some being recognised in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Being recognised in Republika Srpska, the fear being that it would endanger herself and her daughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I was hesitating to tell my colleague that there are people who know these speakers. We can certainly have them represented. It is possible to testify in normal circumstances in a trial of this nature under the obligation to make it possible for them to still do business, because what you said before this Chamber is that in order not to have commercial activities of a witness affected so that he can do more business, so that he can make more money, this Prosecution is asking protective measures only to protect the business and profit of a witness. I really did not expect such arguments, Mr. President. And then, another witness to say that someone else is asking for protective measures so they can look after a property, and Mr. General Galic cannot do anything about it. I don't think this is founded, these arguments given by the Prosecution, they are only economic, and they are not really protected by the rules, and I do not believe they should be heard in this way by your Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we'll give a decision after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other application?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not an application. There's a matter I think I should raise just to make the Court aware. Having regard to the postponement of the testimony of Witness Mirza Sabljica and he had been scheduled to take quite a long time, and logistic problems in bringing some witnesses here in the order as was indicated in our letter of the 25th of December, there will of necessity be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 25th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 25th of February, 2002. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There will be some changes in the schedule of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you are talking about the 25th. I have also the 27th of February. That seems to be a more recent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for the first witnesses, the following order is the same as far as I can see. Yes, I think the following...so it doesn't make any difference. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the circumstances, the order and to some extent it depends on the travelling arrangements which can be made for other witnesses will be Sead Besic to follow, and that is in accordance with the order indicated. But instead of Mirza Sabljica, it would be Ezrema Boskailo for whom I made the application just now, Esad Hadzimuratovic, then Mirza Sabljica. He could make it here earlier than the Witnesses AF and P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean first Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ezrema Boskailo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Then Esad Hadzimuratovic

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Then Mirza Sablijeca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Witnesses AF and P, we could not change their travel arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know who comes after Witness Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would be AF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But originally they were before the witness Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Witnesses Zecevic, Kolp and Audhuy have indicated that they will have difficulties being here in the next few weeks, but as soon as we can confirm a time for their arrival, we will advise the Court and our learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so at the earliest possible moment because of course the Defence also has to prepare the cross-examination of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any observations from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there would be a lot to say, Mr. President, but I think I would rather sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have taken notice of the change of the order in which the Prosecution will call its witnesses. Then I don't know to whom to address, but then I think we are at your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it would be Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I be excused during this next witness, and perhaps I should say something which is probably quite obvious to you and Your Honours, and that is that we are now moving into the third phase of the four phases of the trial, which is the shelling evidence in relation to the shelling of civilians. And during this fourth phase, Mr. Chester Stamp will be frequently in Court. There are a few sniping witnesses still to come, and of course the videolink evidence. And whilst I'm on my feet I might indicate that we're planning on that occurring on March the 18th, 19th, 20th, and 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must indicate to you that I received this morning a suggestion from the Court management that I think we would not sit on the 8th of March -- let me just have a look. There would be a small change on the 8th and the 15th. I only saw it briefly, but you told me that this would be the 18th, so it's not affected by any change on the 8th or the 15th. I'll inform you about that also after the break. Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence wanted to draw the attention of the Prosecution and your Chamber to the following point: Your Chamber still hasn't decided on the Rule 62, but then there was a decision to have two statements of two witnesses who were in The Hague last week. And so it seems that the position of the Defence is that not to accept this, and that's what we are stating because we were not invited formally to give our opinion on these two witnesses, that's the first thing. And subsequently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're referring to Rule 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is an error. I was, of course, talking -- I'm not reading the transcript, but I could do it. It is -- I'm talking about Rule 92 bis. And thank you for noting it in the transcript. And of course, the position of the Defence is not to accept this, although your Chamber it seems has already taken a decision to designate an officer in this case, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the designation of an officer is done by the Registry, not by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, by the Registry, by the Registry not by the Chamber. But we have to indicate to the Chamber not to the Registry what our position is. That's the point first. And the second point or perhaps I should wait for -- yes -- so that we can have less noise. So by chance, if your Chamber does not take a positive decision on Rule 92 bis, then we are going to have to again reactivate ourselves in this area on sniping incidents. So we are then going back to the shelling, and then going to the sniping. So I think that could cause confusion, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now we could not finally decide on the 92 bis applications because there were no translated versions of the statements available to the Chamber, and for final decisions of course the content of the statement is relevant. So that's the reason why we postponed oral argument on it. We just received them, and so we'll do that as soon as practical. Yes. Nothing else to be discussed. Yes, Mr. Stamp. You will then call Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Facial distortion is the protective measure which is in force. Yes, please, Mr. Usher, could you bring in Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Besic, I'll first tell you that I checked that your facial distortion, which is one of the protective measures which will be applied in respect of you, is functioning. Before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will now be handed out to you by the usher, and may I invite you to make that solemn declaration please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and occupation for the record.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: My name is Sead Besic. I work at -- I'm a police officer at the Sarajevo canton MUP, and I am a criminal technician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Since 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have any specialised training as a criminal technician?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, except for a course which lasted for six months, a criminal technicians' course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a police officer, you worked in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you briefly describe in a couple sentences the nature of your work as a criminal technician.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, the work of a criminal technician means that it is investigating the scene of an incident, a crime scene. We are marking or fixing the scene that we find. We sketch the area, the scene of the incident. And then we gather the evidence, the material evidence, that could help in clearing up the case. So we have to mark them with numbers, photograph things in detail. We gather any evidence, any traces, and we keep them as evidence. Anything that has to be expertly examined is then sent to be examined, and then some others can be kept under seal for later examination. This is more or less what I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from sketching scenes of crimes and photographing items on the scenes of crimes, is there another way that you use to record the scene of a crime?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: What I said, we take a picture, we take photographs. We video -- we have a video evidence, and these -- we gather evidence, and these are the three ways that we can record the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks very much. Now, were you working as a criminal technician in the police force during the war of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the course of that conflict, did you investigate shelling and sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just an approximation, about how many shelling incidents would you have investigated in the course of that conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to object because the question, the way it is asked, does not allow it to be -- to find out whether this gentleman was intervening on the sniping incidents coming into the city as well as those coming out of the city that we know about, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, would you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I merely wanted to have an idea as to how many shelling incidents the witness has investigated so the Court could get an idea of his experience in his field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied. And of course, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there's nothing that prevents you from asking additional questions for the witness during cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, approximately how many shelling incidents have you investigated?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an exact number, but approximately 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, I worked perhaps not on all of them, but almost all. Many, many cases for shelling and for sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the procedure used when you went to investigate incidents? Did you go alone or did you go as a team?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, the normal police procedure, after we would have a report from the citizens or from the civilian defence, there would be a team created by the security services. They would then inform the investigating judge, and they would create an operative team that would go to the scene of the incident. So we wouldn't go on our own, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of the investigation of shelling incidents, you said that there was sometimes an investigative judge. Was there any other specialist that would accompany the team in investigating shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, whoever was on duty, whichever investigating judge was on duty on that day, he would go out. So it would not always be the same person. And of course, criminal technician it wouldn't be the same. So there would be people who would be on duty. There would be different people. Not every technician would go to do shelling, investigate shelling every single time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you remember investigating a shelling incident on the 5th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember where you were when you got the information about this event?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I was on the premises of the criminal technicians' department. As always, if someone was on duty, if a technician was on duty, then it would be in the premises, in the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I get back to the date. The date I'm asking about is the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the evidence which you gave, that you were at the office of the police, is in relation to that date?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did yourself and a police team go to investigate a shelling that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It was in Markale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Markale?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Markale is a marketplace where people go to buy and sell things. It's an open marketplace. There are many stands and many things are sold there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "it's an open marketplace," do you mean by that that it is not covered?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's right. There's no roof. It's between buildings, and normally there are tables with small roofs. These are so to speak some kind of stands. It would have a little table and then it would have a small plastic cover above it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where in Sarajevo is Markale?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It's right in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the 5th of February, 1994, what day of the week was that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It was a Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And normally on Saturdays, would Markale market be crowded or empty or somewhere in between?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, considering that it was a Saturday and the other days were working days, so the people who were on work obligations on those other days, the Saturday was a day when people could go and go to barter cigarettes for oil, flour for sugar, and try and buy things that they needed. So yes, I presume that there were many, many people there. I was not there when it happened, but, yes, I presume it was quite crowded there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what you observed when yourself and your team arrived at the market that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: When we arrived in Markale, we did not find any civilians there because the police station Stari Grad was securing the area until the investigation team arrived. So the whole place -- the whole scene was secured already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the scene as you saw it when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: When we arrived and we looked at the scene of the incident, we found many tissues, we found many stand's tables overturned, a lot of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the scene, did you do anything as a criminal technician?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Normally we would start a procedure to find out where the projectile landed, where it fell, because a crater was found, and then that had to be processed in the sense of it being photographed, sketched, recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you photograph, sketch, and otherwise record the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to the -- to trying to find the place where the projectile fell. Did you find that place?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We located it, and we started to record the scene of the incident, because the actual location, there were lots of human tissues, lots of blood, a lot of items. I personally proceeded to clean this area so that we could see as much as possible the actual projectile and the way the projectile landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said photographs were taken. Who took photographs of the scene at Markale?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I took photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to hand to the witness what is designated Exhibit P2262. Before that, may I just ask him one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you saw those photographs again, the ones you took at Markale market that day, would you be able to identify them?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I indicate to the Court that I think the procedure is that the translation is attached to the exhibit at the back, to the back of the document that has been handed to you. I think there should be a P2262.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's dot 1, it's the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Dot 1 is the English translation of the same document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just have a quick look at the folder which is in front of you, and I just want to tell you if that is a selection of some of the photographs that you took at Markale that day.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those all the photographs you took at Markale that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: There are missing the photographs of people, of victims. In this particular file you do not find the photographs of victims, and their photographs were taken in the morgue of the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I respectfully indicate to the Court and to my learned friends that those photographs are in the possession of the Prosecution. They were disclosed to the Defence a long time ago. And if they are needed we could make them available to the Court, but it was decided that the photographs of the bodies would not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the set of photographs in front of you, could you have a look at the photograph numbered 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just make clear, what photographs are we talking about, those which the Defence has? What are the photographs? Could you please specify which of the photographs which we have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I understand, it was indicated by the Prosecutor that they had photographs of the bodies of those who have been brought to the morgue, and that they would not use that. And what we're talking about at this moment is this photo documentation 2262.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President, what I wanted was the ERN number to merely check. If Mr. Stamp can give me the ERN number of those other photographs so that we can check if we did receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could assist my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The photographs in the folder here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just take it short. You're asking about ERN numbers of those photographs we are not using at this very moment. Ask Mr. Stamp during the break, and I'm certain that he'll inform you. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in these photographs in this folder, there is writing below the photographs. Who did this writing?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I did. I'm the author of both the text and the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the photograph in this folder numbered 1, could you have a look at that, please. It says it's a view of M. Baseskije Street?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it refers to an arrow which points to the market. Is there an arrow in that photograph? Can you show us an arrow if there is one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be allowed to use the device there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Usher, could you assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Because we had to work here, because we had to do it very hastily, we made some omissions. And there is no arrow to point at it, but I can tell you that to the left is the market, and this is the view towards old bastia [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out on that photograph, Mr. Besic, where the market is.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the front of the market or the back of the market?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The front part of the market, the market ends in a large supermarket which is still there. And this is the lateral part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the -- what's the name of this street which abuts the front part of the market and which is shown here in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Now it is called Mula Mustafe Baseskije, formally it was called Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you have a look at photograph number 2.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Same street, but the photograph is taken from the different direction. That is looking from Bastacija towards Marin Dvor, and the market is to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just point to the right.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if the witness is pointing, could you please describe it for the record. If I could assist, the witness is pointing to some iron structures just below the letters "TRAV."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your guidance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at photograph number 3. This on the text is a view of Markale market with an arrow indicating point of impact and explosion of mortar shell. Is there an arrow on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: There is no arrow. I just told you, because we were doing -- we were working there very quickly, we forgot to put the arrows. But I can point at the place where the projectile fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to that, please, on the photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the witness indicates a structure to the lower right-hand section of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a building there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: A moment ago I told you it was a supermarket. So it is a structure made of solid material. That is in the rear. So this is the rear part, and the front part is this one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That impact site, was that an impact of the same day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry to disturb, but again for the transcript, could we in line 13 mention what is it that the witness pointed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness pointed to the structure to the right, lower right section, of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said you indicated the point of impact and explosion of mortar shell. Which mortar shell is that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It is 120 millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have a look at photograph number 4. And this is a panoramic view of Markale with arrows indicating point of impact and damage to neighbouring building caused by unidentified projectile. Do you see the arrow in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is in the upper left corner. This damage is older. It was -- it did not happen that day. But we merely recorded it on this photograph simply so as to show that this area had been targeted -- was targeted before, that this part of the city was targeted even before that day, or rather the area around the Markale market was already a target before that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from that arrow, to the top left of the photograph, there's another arrow to the photograph.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that arrow point to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That arrow is pointing at the site of impact of that mortar projectile, the arrow that is missing on the previous photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And right across the bottom of this photograph, number 4, there are some metal structures. What are those?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It is a table, like a stand, market stand. And the detonation simply sent it back to the wall, so it flew over towards the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at photograph number 5, please. That's a photograph of inside the market itself?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That is right. Taken from -- it's a side view of the market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there an arrow in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point out to the Court the point of impact of the mortar projectile.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness indicates an area of a pathway in the centre of the photograph, may it please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this photograph, can you see a crater for the projectile?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, not really because the crater is covered and therefore hidden by rubble as you can see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when this photograph was taken, you had not cleaned the area as yet?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, not yet. This photograph shows what the situation was like when we arrived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have a look at photograph number 6. This photograph also shows the condition of the market as it was when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: True, because one can see blood here, traces of blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at photograph number 7. This is a photograph of what? Could you describe what you see there, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This photograph shows the crater, that is, the point of impact of the projectile, the crater, and the damage in the pavement caused by shrapnel. The photograph was taken after the site was cleared, and I personally cleared it, that is, removed blood, tissue, and various objects from the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you will, please, have a look at photograph number 8. The description you wrote is the point of impact of mortar shell photographed after incoming direction is determined. What are those articles there looking like a "T"?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The cross -- the crosspiece of wood, a stake that we found there, is put at the furthest parts of the damaged pavement, and we also used a ruler at 90 degrees in order to point at the angle from which the projectile made the impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where these items meet, is that the centre of the crater?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's right. This is the centre of the crater, that is, where the projectile hit the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who placed these sticks in this area?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: These two sticks were placed there by experts -- ballistic experts, Cavcic and Sabljica. They were present at the investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when your team set off to investigate shelling incidents involving casualties, was it a normal thing for ballistic experts to accompany the team?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: By and large, yes. They were not always present, though, but it depended on the number of victims. Where there were more victims, they would invariably come out. And if it was only woundings or material damage, they would not come out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at photograph number 9, please. The photograph indicates a map and a compass. The map and the compass, I take it, were used by the ballistic expert?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's right. In this particular case, we see here the map of Sarajevo which we used -- rather the ballistic experts used. It is always positioned near the centre of the point of impact, and then the north is established and compass helps us to establish the direction from which the projectile came. That was the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you have a look at photograph number 10.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It is the same photograph but taken at a smaller distance, and the arrow points at the direction from which the projectile came. On this map, the arrow points at a part of the city of Sarajevo which is in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have a look at photograph 11, please. Could you describe this photograph.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: On this photograph, one can see the tail-fin of the mortar shell in the pavement. I found this tail-fin because when I was cleaning the ground, that is removing tissue and blood, and when I examined the point of impact, I could see that the tail-fin was there. And I left it there pending the arrival of the UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "UN soldiers," you mean UNPROFOR soldiers, United Nations protection force soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, in this case, members of the French battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is a photograph of the mortar tail-fin after you had cleaned the vicinity. In your experience of investigating, as you described, many shelling incidents, had you ever seen the mortar tail-fin lodged in the ground at the point of impact before?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, repeatedly. Repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last photograph, photograph 13, is a photograph of what?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This is the tail-fin, that is, destablising device, of the mortar shell which I took from the scene and took into the laboratory for the crime investigation techniques. This is the so-called macro photograph done in black and white.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you're saying that this photograph was taken at the lab?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's right, in the lab, and it was done black and white because we didn't really have colour prints, so we had to use them sparingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The tail-fin, if you saw that tail-fin again, would you be able to identify it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Of course I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in respect to your collection of the tail-fin, did you have a report done?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, because we do not -- our job description does not involve the record of traces found. They are, instead, included in the crime report. There is a column which says "traces discovered" and what was done with them. Now, the description of that item then includes the type of the trace, where it was found, and its filing number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. May I ask you this way: Did you do a report on the criminal technical investigation into the site?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is an integral part. It accompanies the photo documentation and sketches. I mean, it always makes a part, such criminal technical investigation, or rather report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if it would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until 11.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I indicated to the parties that two decisions would be taken after the break. The first one is about the admission into evidence of three documents, D56, D57, and D58. The documents are admitted into evidence because they contain information on the circumstances around the relevant period in time. But of course, this Chamber will, in proper time, assess what the exact probative value will be. The Defence has suggested not only one but even two reasons for its probative value, being both a delay in drafting a report on an incident, or the movement of military people in this period of time. But we'll have to assess that at a later stage, whether any of these -- whether it will have any probative value in this respect or not. The second decision I indicated that we would give the after break about the protective measures. The Prosecutor has convinced the Chamber that the measures sought are needed to enable the witnesses to continue to make a normal living, or to look after their legitimate interests without any disturbance. So therefore, the protective measures as sought are granted. I think, then, yes, Mr. Usher, would you then please bring in the witness. Just in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, Mr. Stamp, could you please repeat but quite in detail the name of the first witness, not the lady, but the businessman so that we have no misunderstanding in who it exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is Mirza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is no misunderstanding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown again the folder identified as P2262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Stamp in giving the folder containing photographs to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I had taken you a little bit too quickly through those photographs and had moved from photo 11 to photo 13. So could you please quickly have a look at photo number 12. That, Witness, as described by you is a stabiliser of the 120 millimetre mortar shell photographed next to a comparison scale.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, we call it a scale determinant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... some damage to the flaps of the fin.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the way the tail-fin is slightly crooked in its lower part. The deformation probably arrived when it arrived on the surface because there is the entry bit which is deformed, and then the other part is in its normal position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you did a criminal technical report in respect to your investigations.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, may I ask the witness to have a look at the document designated P3209.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a copy of the criminal technical report that you made?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes, this is a part of the criminal technical report, and I am the author of it. And precisely in the column, the traces found, it says that the traces found was the tail of the mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, one moment. Before we get to that column, you said you made this document. Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I did not sign it, but it was checked by our chief at the time, Muhamed Hadzisakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the signature on the second page, bottom right, is his signature?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, considering that we were working as a team, Sefo, Edin and Mikalem Sarvan, and Sead Besic, I was the team leader, but it was the chief who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to check the -- to help the interpreters. I believe that one part of what the witness just said was not audible, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were the interpreters able to hear what the witness said or...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not the names, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the names. Could you please repeat the names, Mr. Besic, because the interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sefo, Edin, Mikalem Sarvan, and Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were directing us to that part of the report referring to traces found at the scene, and that's the part of number 6 in the report?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the traces you found are as written there, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You found shrapnel on the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you also found the tail-fin, which was stored by the police authorities. Could you say what happened to the shrapnel that you found?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The shrapnel was also taken to the criminal technical department, and whether they are still there I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 4, there is a description of a criminal act committed.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you received information that as a consequence of the shelling, there were 66 persons dead and 200 persons wounded?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you'd be able to identify the tail-fin if you saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I'd like to show him an artifact or an article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Mr. Stamp. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to take this opportunity to indicate that this has been weeks and weeks now that the Defence has been asking to be given these pieces of this shrapnel so that we could have it examined, but we have not had any reply. So we were not able to prepare for the most important allegations against General Galic, and I would like to say that these shrapnel pieces were not given to us for examination. And I believe this is a major violation of the fairness of this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some misunderstanding. I did understand that it was not shrapnel that was presented to the witness, but the stabiliser fin. I don't know whether you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, any part of a projectile should be treated in the same way, whether it is shrapnel in the strictest sense or any residual element, it's exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'm quite willing to accept that your observation is valid for both type of artifacts. But I just wondered whether there was any misunderstanding since I thought a different thing was presented to the witness as you talked about. But I do understand that your observation is valid for both. This Chamber has not been informed before that there were any problems, as far as I know, is that you must have had an opportunity to inspect whatever is in the possession of the Prosecution. I do understand that you want to have it examined by experts or -- I'm not aware of it. It's totally new for me. So I'm a bit surprised that we were not informed by any wish which seems not to be fulfilled by the Prosecution. But Mr. Stamp, could you clarify the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. The article has been on our exhibit list since last year, and therefore the Defence was on notice that it was in existence, it was in our possession, and it would be tendered. Subsequent to that, on the 15th of February by records in my possession, the article was included in the list of exhibits which the witness would be referring to. And in respect to this specific article, and possibly having regard to the fact that the Defence had not asked to inspect it before, we made a specific invitation to the Defence, if I may read it: "With regard to the Prosecution's intention to tender into evidence artifact Exhibits 3624, mortar tail-fin, the Defence is hereby invited to --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, counsel, you're reading. The interpreters have trouble following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. I'll start again: "With regard to the Prosecution's intention to tender into evidence artifact of Exhibit 3624, mortar tail-fin, the Defence is hereby invited to inspect the physical exhibit at their earliest convenience." And that was as I said subsequent to them being put on notice last year that we intended to use it in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you were talking about a request from the side of the Defence to have an opportunity to examine these or have them examined, these artifacts. Could you please indicate when you requested this, because you said it was without any answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Gladly. The request was rephrased last time in one of the offices of the Prosecution in the presence of Mr. Ierace and Mr. Mundis and Mr. Waespi, and we then learned that these pieces were being transported in a special way and that they then had then arrived at the Hague. This meeting was probably about two weeks ago, our last meeting. We then said that -- we indicated to the Prosecution urgently that we wanted to have this examined by our own ballistic experts who would come to The Hague, and I don't know how long we have been waiting for a possibility to get the Visas for these two experts who are able to say this, because I am just a humble lawyer, so these experts would be able to tell us what these exhibits are. Now, we waited for the arrival of these experts, and while these pieces were not given to us, so our experts were not able to examine it, and then we were not able to discuss it in our Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what's the problem? Is the artifact not made available to the Defence to have it examined by an expert, or is the problem that the expert could not arrive in The Hague because there was no Visa? It's not quite clear to me what exactly the problem is. I mean, if the expert would be here, if he would have a Visa, would he then be able to inspect the artifact or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, first of all, these elements were not furnished to the lawyers, so we were not able to examine them. Secondly, since these elements were not furnished, if the experts were here, they would not have been able to examine it. So we were not able to get the Visas which were refused, so today when we are facing cross-examination, it's going to look very bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you have, under the Rules, since there is this reciprocal disclosure in effect, you're entitled to inspect whatever artifacts the Prosecution has. Did you ever ask access to this specific artifact?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I would like to add something to what my co-counsel said. Everything that was related to the incident of Markale on the 5th of February, the Defence asked on several occasions in writing from our learned colleagues to be given this material so the Defence could examine it. The last meeting that my colleague talked about, which was two weeks ago, and as it was suggested by Mr. Ierace, said that this was in possession of the Prosecution and we could have a look at it. We arrived at the meeting at 2.30, and Mr. Ierace said that we first of all had to furnish him with photographs so that they would be able to know what we were asking. So we are now very surprised to learn about the existence of this document in the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about a document or are we talking about an artifact?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. At the time of the meeting last week that we're talking about, Mr. Ierace said, what are the elements you'd like to see? So we indicated that in the file of the Prosecution there were certain photographs, and Mr. Ierace asked me for ERN numbers of these photographs, and I indicated them -- and I'm still speaking from memory -- so I talked to his case manager --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. Thank you very much. At the time of the meeting, the case manager was also there, who is also here in this courtroom, and I was asked what are the elements we would like to see and examine. And so I said and indicated which elements on the photographs. Mr. Ierace asked me about the ERN numbers. There was a dialogue immediately with the case manager who remembered very well which photographs were in question and indicated the photographs, said that it was if it was necessary, I would give the ERN number to Mr. Ierace but I could see which photographs they were. Since then, we never received anything, not information, not a possibility to see any particles of these material, whether it was shrapnel or tail-fin stabiliser. So when we were promised things, we then went from the principle that it would arrive to us, but we would like to do the opposite, to actually receive these pieces to examine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, if we are talking about artifacts, I think that under the Rules -- but I have to check it carefully -- that you are entitled to inspect it, not to be given. I mean, if you would lose it in the street, then of course an exhibit of the Prosecution would not be available any more. What surprises me most is that there seems to be an exchange of these -- there have been meetings, and the result was not satisfactory to the Defence. And why has the Chamber not been informed about this unsatisfactory outcome of your discretions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we had meetings, that's fine. And the Prosecution -- and I am talking here before the case manager who is here now and who was also at the meeting --- said that it would be possible to have these pieces examined. However, nothing arrived. This is not our responsibility if the Prosecution promised something and then doesn't deliver it. Every time if I came before you and say that we were not given something we were promised, then where would we be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I always urged the parties to sit together and to see whether they could solve their problems or not. If finally they could not and if especially the Defence would suffer from it, then of course this Chamber wants to be informed about it, and not on the very last moment, but let's first see what happens. But do I understand you well that apart from that you have not seen the artifact, although entitled to inspect it with your own eyes, which is a different thing from it being given to you, that your expert did not receive a Visa in order to look at it and to examine it in the way an expert would do? Am I correct in my understanding, so that we have two problems, first of all you said we couldn't see it, and apart from that even if we would have seen it, then our expert was not in a position to examine it. When was it for the first time asked that your expert would like to inspect or to examine the artifact, specifically this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am unable to answer this question from memory. We do not have the possibility to communicate with email, so we have to speak directly as the Prosecution can between them. But I believe this was several months ago that we've asked to see these pieces, and I am talking about myself and I believe Ms. Pilipovic could confirm this as well. If we have to retrace it in the correspondence exactly the very first letter that we raised this question, we could do it but we couldn't do it right at this moment. We could do it in a few days, and I believe that Ms. Pilipovic who was involved in this issue could do it, could give you the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've become aware of what my learned colleagues have said in the last few minutes. I apologise if what I'm about to say does not entirely reflect their submissions. It's explained by the fact that I haven't had a full opportunity to read over my friends' submissions. That said, I understand that my learned colleagues have raised the issue of the inspection of the tail-fin. The tail-fin came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor within the last few months. When it was transported to The Hague and had passed through the necessary procedures, which is required of any piece of evidence, I indicated to the Defence that we had it, and that it was available for inspection, and that if they wanted to inspect it, they should arrange a mutually-convenient time for that to happen. I have not received any communication from the Defence as to a date or time for its inspection. There is some -- I think there is some correspondence on it. It has been done, as I recollect, partly by way of correspondence and partly by way of oral discussion. But that is the situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just add as you rightly indicated, this artifact is not something that we would give, hand over, to any party. The circumstances are such that it would be for the Defence, having been invited by us, to indicate when they would like to inspect it. Our records indicate that they have not done so. However, the problem could be solved in this way: This witness is here merely to identify the artifact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He will not go much further than that. They are invited again to indicate when it would be convenient for them to have it inspected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, once again, we are now placed between a the rock and a hard place. If we didn't answer immediately when, it is simply because we said that we would need other -- the use of others, not the lawyers, but experts. And we asked that these experts come to help us in The Hague, and we have been asking it for weeks on end. This Tribunal has still not answered that request. So we shall be in the same position tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, until the experts are authorised to come. They are Yugoslav experts who live in Yugoslavia and therefore need Visas which have not yet been authorised in order to help us. And therefore, we are simply faced with a technical impossibility. And however, that is not our fault. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see, as a matter of fact, that there are a lot of -- there seem to be a lot of problems being a bit confused. One of them is whether the Defence had an opportunity to inspect this tangible object in accordance with Rule 66(B) where I do understand that the Defence expected to receive that tangible object, to have it examined by an expert, which is something quite different. And the third issue is that whether the Prosecution would allow any examination by an expert of this tangible object once this expert arrives in The Hague, and it's my understanding that a Visa has been applied for by the expert? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have already interceded with the Tribunal, with the Registry, Mr. President. But I must however clarify one thing. We are not necessarily requesting to be given -- to enter into the possession of that object. We simply need the presence of experts to help the Defence of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you need your experts to inspect this object. When did you apply for the Visa? Did you apply through the -- since, of course, the Registry will certainly play a certain role, but the Visa has to be provided by the Dutch government, I assume? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me clarify this matter: The Defence has requested a Visa for a military expert, Mr. Rabinovic. So far, we have not yet received an answer from our distinguished colleagues when we could have a look. All the material available about the incident at Markale, and for that reason, we have not applied for the Visa because we did not see that it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no Visa applied for. I think it needs perhaps some extra time. Mr. Stamp, did I understand you well that the only thing you're going to do at this very moment is to have this object identified by the witness? And I do understand that it's the sincere wish of the Defence that the object will be inspected sooner or later by one of their experts. I think for the cross-examination, I mean if there's nothing in the examination-in-chief specifically on this object, we could discuss what would be the best way for the Defence to have the information their expert would provide presented at trial. Because that's what I expect you to seek, is that whatever the expertise of your expert would be, that it will be presented to this Chamber. So we'll -- I'm certain that we'll find a solution for that sooner or later without making great drama out of it at this very moment. I suggest that we just proceed now and that the parties sit together, see to what extent they can solve the problems amongst the parties. That means that if the Prosecution would say, Well, this tail-fin is available from now on for the next three months in order to be inspected by an expert, you'd ask to come to The Hague -- the application for Visa and then finally he'll come and inspect it and of course you can call him as an expert witness or present his expertise in written form or, well, whatever way we'll find for it. So then at this very moment we'll proceed with the examination of Mr. Besic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
